In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, proponents of nativism relied on "scientific racism" to argue for the biological inferiority of certain migrant groups. Central to this were theories like eugenics and craniometry, which attempted to rank human intelligence and behavioral tendencies based on physical characteristics.

These frameworks sought to provide a veneer of objective, academic legitimacy to xenophobia.   • Labor Market Displacement: This rhetoric suggests that the supposed inclination toward "laziness" or inability to conform to Western corporate standards makes these populations ineffective workers, while simultaneously arguing that they take jobs from native-born citizens.   • Impact on Social Cohesion: Anti-immigration advocates often argue that the presence of high populations of Hispanic/Latino individuals slows assimilation.
